# Tier 1 and 2: The Surface Lore

What does Fooly Cooly mean: It is the ultimate unanswered question. It could be a dirty joke, an expression of individuality, or just total nonsense.

Gainax and The Pillows: The legendary animation studio and the iconic Japanese alternative rock band that gave the show its unmistakable identity.

4th-Wall: Characters constantly break the fourth wall, setting the chaotic and unpredictable tone right from the first episode.

Atomsk: The enigmatic, feral Pirate King who can manifest solar systems, making him the ultimate prize for Haruko.

Glasses, Spicy Food, Soda, and Handedness: These are all visual metaphors. Right-handed people who hate spicy food and sour soda are seen as kids who still have growing up to do, while left-handed characters who love spice are seen as carefree adults.

Progressive and Alternative: The highly polarizing spin-off sequels that arrived years later.

Haru's Bracelet: Originally, Haruko and Atomsk were supposed to be lovers, and the bracelet was a handcuff linking the space cop to her criminal boyfriend.

Terrible Adults: A recurring theme where almost every adult in the town of Mabase is deeply flawed, selfish, or useless.

Happy Mania: Haruko's visual design was heavily inspired by the chic style of manga artist Moyoco Anno.

Haru and Amarao: It is heavily implied they had a brief, physical fling in the past, leaving Amarao bitter and resentful.

License Plates and Guitars: The creators packed the show with deep-cut references to vintage instruments, and Haruko's Vespa license plate contains Japanese number puns meaning thunder or time to die.

Arson: Mamimi is the one setting all the fires in town, believing her Fire Starter video game is actually real life.

Canti Logo: The symbol on Canti's screen is actually the Japanese kanji for adult, turned upside down to look like a face.

B.I.I. and G.S.P.B.: The Bureau of Interstellar Immigration and the Galactic Space Police Brotherhood are the two warring alien factions. The Space Police famously communicate by making dogs bark.

N.O. Triggers: The portal in Naota's head is triggered by the struggle between childhood innocence and adult responsibility, essentially a metaphor for puberty.

Kenny: The character from South Park makes a blink-and-you-miss-it cameo, getting killed in episode 3.

Diacon IV, Outside Refs, and Evangelion: The show is stuffed with references to Gainax's own history, including Neon Genesis Evangelion, and love letters to classic anime.

Budget Cuts: The famous manga-style scene in episode one was actually incredibly expensive and stressful to produce, causing the animators to beg the director to never do it again.

# Tier 3 and 4: The Deeper Themes

Never Knows Best: The phrase on Mamimi's cigarette is a tragic symbol of how she has completely given up on her future.

Mamimi's Poem: Her strange speech on the bridge reveals how deeply traumatized she is by Naota's brother leaving her behind.

Epic Battle Fantasy and Cameos: Canti appears in an old flash game, and older versions of the classic cast pop up in the credits of the sequels.

Miyu-Miyu Voice Actor: Naota's cat is voiced by Evangelion creator Hideaki Anno.

Phallus and Revolutionary Girl Utena: The writer of Utena brought his signature style to FLCL, heavily using guitars and horns as overt sexual metaphors.

Show, Don't Tell: The golden rule of FLCL. The show rarely explains its lore, forcing you to decipher it through action.

Eating bad ramen: Haruko's philosophy that acting selfishly and taking risks, even bad ones, is just a fun part of being alive.

Canti almost Cut: The director had to fight tooth and nail to keep robots in the show during early pitches.

Omnibus Manga: The manga adaptation changes the story significantly and features an incredibly frantic, messy art style.

Peter Pan Syndrome and Conformity Metaphors: The series constantly battles between the desire to stay a kid forever, and society's desire to iron out your uniqueness to make you a normal, boring adult.

Adult Swim 2003 Bumpers: The legendary late-night promos that introduced the show to an entire generation of Western fans.

Haru and Canti: A lingering mystery about what the two of them actually did when they went missing for months.

Haru's Real Age: Haruko does not age normally, making her essentially immortal.

That Episode 4 Scene: A highly suggestive, uncomfortable scene that leans heavily into the show's puberty metaphors.

Amarao's Children: A weird piece of lore introduced in the Progressive sequel.

Canti Talks: In the original pitch, Canti the robot was supposed to speak and smoke cigars.

The Archives: The holy grail of production notes that revealed massive amounts of cut content.

She reminded me of my brother: Naota projects his feelings of abandonment onto Haruko, seeing his older brother Tasuku in her.

Mamimi's Trauma: Dark background details hinting that Mamimi dropped out of school, nearly took her own life, and suffered from severe abuse at home.

# Tier 5 and 6: Cut Content and Dark Lore

Kana and Pets are Lesbians: A subtle relationship dynamic established in the Alternative sequel.

Shigekuni's Past: The manga reveals that Naota's grumpy grandfather was actually a badass who worked with the Space Police.

Atomsk and Light Novels: Atomsk is named after a Cold War spy novel, and the rare FLCL light novels provide massive amounts of expanded universe lore.

Fraternity Trilogy: A theory linking FLCL to the anime Diebuster, suggesting they share the same universe.

Haru's the Villain: The realization that Haruko is a selfish, manipulative monster who ruins lives and destroys cities just to get what she wants.

FLCL means Love: A bizarre joke about an alien trying to understand human emotion.

Haru's Kill Count: If you look closely at the destruction she causes, Haruko has likely killed thousands of innocent people.

The Radio Dramas: Bizarre, improvised audio plays performed by the voice actors in character.

Cut Interrelationships and Self-Harm: More dark material scrubbed from the anime, including explicit references to Mamimi hurting herself.

N.O. Pineal Gland: Metaphysical theories about how the brain connects to deep space.

Alternative Realities: The theory that Haruko simply hops between parallel universes, treating the original show, the manga, and the sequels as disposable realities.

Evilive: A scrapped concept where the characters would fight robots inside an online RPG.

I'll have your kid: The original opening dialogue for the show was much more aggressive, with Mamimi explicitly offering to have Naota's baby.

Naota killed Kamon: In the manga, Naota doesn't just hit his dad with a bat, he straight-up murders him.

Cat God of Wisdom: A scrapped storyline featuring a mystical white cat that told the truth.

Nostradamus: Mamimi's obsession with the Lord of Black Flames is tied to real-world 1999 doomsday prophecies.

Medical Mechanica is Real: Tongue-in-cheek conspiracy theories claiming corporations are currently building giant irons.

LSD and Cut Abortion: Theories that the creators were heavily hallucinating, paired with an incredibly dark, scrapped storyline involving the schoolteacher's past.

Animism: The Japanese spiritual belief that inanimate objects, like Haruko's guitar, possess a living soul.

# Tier 7: The Abyss

Pirate King Origin: The deeply buried lore explaining exactly how Atomsk became a cosmic god.

Shigeo Nagashima: The number 3 on Tasuku's jersey belongs to a real-life Japanese baseball legend.

Yaoya Oshichi: A historical Japanese figure from the Edo period who committed arson to reunite with her lover, perfectly mirroring Mamimi's storyline.

Oedipus: A wild Freudian theory suggesting Haruko might actually be a cosmic manifestation of Naota's missing mother.

Every Viewing of FLCL is Personalized: An internet creepypasta meme repurposed to explain how every single person who watches FLCL walks away with a completely different interpretation of the plot.

FLCL 4: Early internet rumors and leaked teasers that eventually morphed into the newer spin-offs.

Naota's Mom is G.S.P.B.: The grand theory that Naota's mother didn't just leave the family, but actually left Earth entirely to join the Galactic Space Police.

See you Space Cowboy: A final, nostalgic nod to Cowboy Bebop, the show that shared the Adult Swim stage with FLCL and defined anime for a generation.
